claim: About 2 Mha of Amazonian forests are disturbed by selective logging each year.
source: When 2 Mha of Amazonian forests are disturbed by selective logging each year, more than 90 Tg of carbon (C) is emitted to the atmosphere.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a factual assertion about the extent of selective logging.

claim: More than 90 Tg of carbon is emitted to the atmosphere from selective logging in Amazonian forests each year.
source: When 2 Mha of Amazonian forests are disturbed by selective logging each year, more than 90 Tg of carbon (C) is emitted to the atmosphere.

claim: Net aboveground carbon recovery over 10 years is higher in the Guiana Shield and in the west (21 ±3 Mg C ha-1) than in the south (12 ±3 Mg C ha-1).
source: We show that net aboveground C recovery over 10 years is higher in the Guiana Shield and in the west (21 ±3 Mg C ha-1) than in the south (12 ±3 Mg C ha-1) where environmental stress is high (low rainfall, high seasonality).
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract with specific quantitative values derived from the study's modeling approach.

claim: Environmental stress in southern Amazonia is high due to low rainfall and high seasonality.
source: We show that net aboveground C recovery over 10 years is higher in the Guiana Shield and in the west (21 ±3 Mg C ha-1) than in the south (12 ±3 Mg C ha-1) where environmental stress is high (low rainfall, high seasonality).
evidence: This is stated as an explanation for the lower carbon recovery in the south.

claim: Survivors play a key role in forest regrowth after selective logging.
source: We highlight the key role of survivors in the forest regrowth and elaborate a comprehensive map of post-disturbance C recovery potential in Amazonia.
evidence: This is stated as a key finding in the abstract.

claim: Most selectively logged forests remain as forested areas.

claim: The study used long-term (8–30 year) inventory data from 13 experimentally-disturbed sites across Amazonia.
source: Based on long-term (8–30 year) inventory data from 13 experimentally-disturbed sites (Sist et al., 2015) across Amazonia (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), 133 permanent forest plots (175 ha in total) that cover a large gradient of disturbance intensities (ACS losses ranging from 1% to 71%) were used to model the trajectory of those post-disturbance ACS changes (Figure 1) in a comprehensive Bayesian framework.
evidence: This describes the data used in the study with a citation to Sist et al., 2015.

claim: The study used 133 permanent forest plots totaling 175 ha.

claim: A 40% ACS loss is a common disturbance intensity after conventional logging in Amazonia.
source: With global maps of ACS (Avitabile et al., 2016), climatic conditions (Hijmans et al., 2005) and soil bulk density (Nachtergaele et al., 2008), we up-scale our results to Amazonia (sensu lato) and elaborate predictive maps of potential ACS changes over 10 years under the hypothesis of a 40% ACS loss, which is a common disturbance intensity after conventional logging in Amazonia (Blanc et al., 2009; Martin et al., 2015; West et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Blanc et al., 2009; Martin et al., 2015; West et al., 2014.

claim: Disentangling ACS recovery into demographic processes and cohorts is essential to reveal mechanisms underlying ACS responses to disturbance.
source: Disentangling ACS recovery into demographic processes and cohorts is essential to reveal mechanisms underlying ACS responses to disturbance and to make more robust predictions of ACS recovery compared to an all-in-one approach (see Appendix).
evidence: This is stated as a methodological justification.

claim: Net ACS change stays high longer at high disturbance intensity.

claim: Central Amazonia is a transition zone for the main environmental and biotic gradients found in Amazonia.
source: Finally, Central Amazonia is a transition zone for the main environmental and biotic gradients found in Amazonia: (1) a competition gradient between dense and nutrient-poor northeastern forests and nutrient-rich western forests; (2) an environmental gradient between northern wet forests and southern drier forests (Quesada et al., 2012).

claim: Across Amazonia, survivors contribute most to post-disturbance ACS recovery.

claim: Because of the slow tree growth rates in Amazonia, many trees will not reach the 20 cm DBH threshold 10 years after logging.

evidence: This is an inference based on citations to Vieira et al., 2005 and Herault et al., 2010.

claim: High disturbance intensities result in lower survivors' ACS growth.
